To predicate something means to establish it on a specific foundation — to say that one thing rests on, depends on, or is made valid by something else. That foundation isn't optional background. It is the very thing the first thing requires in order to stand. Remove the foundation, and what was built on top of it collapses or becomes invalid.

A simple way to hold this in your head: when something is predicated on something else, the second thing is the ground, and the first thing is the building standing on it. The building doesn't just happen to touch the ground — it needs that ground to exist.

In everyday use, you'll almost always encounter this word in the passive construction: "X is predicated on Y." This means X is logically grounded in Y, or X is only valid because Y is assumed to be true.

Look at these examples, and pay attention to how the dependency works:

"His business plan is predicated on the assumption that people will pay $50 for the product."
→ His entire plan rests on that assumption. If the assumption turns out to be wrong, the plan doesn't just weaken — it becomes invalid at its root.

"Her confidence is predicated on years of hard work."
→ Her confidence is not random. It is grounded in, and justified by, those years of effort. That's its foundation.

"Democracy is predicated on the belief that every citizen deserves a voice."
→ Democracy cannot exist, even in theory, without this belief underneath it. The belief is what makes democracy make sense.

In all three cases, the relationship is not casual or vague. It is a necessary dependency — a logical requirement.

This is a distinction worth knowing precisely, because the two phrases are often used interchangeably — but "predicated on" is stronger and more exact.

When you say something is based on something, you are saying the first thing was influenced by, or grew out of, the second thing. It is a fairly loose connection. A movie "based on a true story" doesn't mean every detail must be true for the movie to make sense.

When you say something is predicated on something, you are saying the first thing logically requires the second thing to be true. It is making a formal claim that the foundation is a necessary condition — not just an influence, but something the thing cannot stand without. If the foundation is false, the thing built on top is not just weakened, it is fundamentally undermined.

So: "based on" suggests origin or influence. "Predicated on" suggests logical dependency — that without the second thing, the first thing has no leg to stand on.
The Second Sense: To Assert a Quality

In more formal, philosophical, or academic contexts, "predicate" as a verb has a related but distinct meaning: to assert or affirm something as a property or quality of something else. To predicate a quality of something is to declare that quality belongs to it.

For example: "We predicate consciousness of all beings that can feel pain."
This means: we assert, or formally claim, that consciousness is a property belonging to pain-feeling beings. We are attaching the concept of consciousness to them as a defining attribute.

Another example: "You cannot predicate honesty of someone who lies habitually."
This means: you cannot meaningfully assert honesty as a quality of a habitual liar.

This usage is less common in everyday conversation, but it appears regularly in philosophy, logic, and linguistics. It is connected to the grammatical term "predicate" (the part of a sentence that says something about the subject), because in grammar, the predicate is what asserts something about the subject. The verb form captures that same act — the act of making an assertion about something.

These two senses may feel different on the surface, but they share a common core: making a deliberate, logical connection between two things.

In the first sense, you are connecting a conclusion or a claim to the foundation it requires to be valid. In the second sense, you are connecting a quality or property to the thing it belongs to. In both cases, "predicate" is not a vague or casual word. It always implies a meaningful, reasoned, formal connection — someone is making a precise claim about how one thing relates to another.

This is what gives the word its particular weight. It is not used for loose associations. It is used when you want to say: this relationship is fundamental, necessary, and deliberate.
A Quick Way to Remember It

Whenever you see or use "predicate" as a verb, ask yourself: what is the thing that makes this valid or possible? That thing is what everything else is predicated on. It's the floor beneath everything else. And if that floor doesn't hold, nothing above it can either.
